claims.text: Low-temperature solid-state reduction of single-source noble-metal precursors restricts metal-atom mobility.
Restricted metal-atom mobility drives stochastic or random incorporation into growing nanoparticles.
Having five or more elements increases the probability of forming a well-mixed, single-phase alloy under limited-mobility conditions.
Binary or low-element mixtures tend to segregate because of sequential reduction and stronger element-specific interactions.
The starting material is a solid, mixed, single-source precursor containing near-equimolar amounts of at least five noble-metal salts.
Moderate reduction temperatures can limit free atomic diffusion in the solid precursor.
Short reduction times and omission of a high-temperature annealing step are required conditions for the proposed mechanism.
Limited mobility forces simultaneous as well as stochastic incorporation of the different metals.
Increasing the number of atom types can promote random alloy formation even when individual element pairs have non-ideal mixing tendencies.
Binary systems have fewer possible incorporation sequences, making them more susceptible to segregation.
Nanoparticles made from five or more noble-metal precursors under the proposed conditions will have a uniform elemental distribution and form a true high-entropy alloy.
Corresponding binary or low-element nanoparticles made under the same conditions will display phase separation or elemental segregation.
The proposed mechanism primarily applies to low-temperature reduction of solid, mixed, single-source precursors.
The mechanism may not apply to solution synthesis or high-temperature annealing where atomic mobility is high.
Element-specific mixing enthalpies can still cause local segregation within an otherwise mixed nanoparticle.
The critical number of elements needed for stochastic mixing may vary with precursor composition and reduction kinetics.
Observation of a homogeneous single-phase binary alloy comparable to the multielement alloy would decisively falsify the proposed statistical advantage.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis presents five elements as the operative threshold, whereas the uncertainty field concedes that the critical element count may vary with composition and kinetics.

The hypothesis and baseline describe binary segregation as a tendency, but the predicted outcome is categorical and the falsification rule treats one homogeneous binary result as decisive. A single successful binary alloy would not by itself refute a probabilistic tendency, especially because the cited evidence explicitly reports single-phase binary formation when reduction is cooperative.
